evidence.supportingExcerpt:
A drug target is a biological molecule or structure that a treatment acts on, and the mechanism of action explains how that action produces an effect. The National Cancer Institute describes targeted therapy as treatment that targets proteins that control how cancer cells grow, divide and spread, and says most targeted therapies are small-molecule drugs, which are small enough to enter cells and so suit targets inside cells, or monoclonal antibodies, which are designed to attach to specific targets on cancer cells. It describes antibodies that mark cancer cells for the immune system, antibodies that stop growth or cause self-destruction directly, and antibodies that carry toxins to cancer cells. These are different jobs, so a shared label of targeted does not make the mechanisms interchangeable, and a target that is only an address for delivery need not drive the cancer's growth.

An altered gene or an elevated protein can suggest a target hypothesis; it does not show that inhibiting the target will harm cancer cells selectively, which controlled perturbations of the target test, and safe exposure and appropriate clinical studies answer later questions. Naming a target answers only the first of several questions. Binding is an interaction between molecules and can be shown with a purified protein, which does not show that the compound reaches the protein inside a cell. Target engagement asks whether the interaction occurs in the relevant cells or tissue, and exposure, target location and the cell membrane all bear on it; a blood concentration and a concentration at an intracellular target are different observations. The cellular thermal shift assay of Martinez Molina and colleagues was developed to evaluate drug binding to target proteins in cells and tissue samples, and its authors used it to monitor drug transport and activation, off-target effects and resistance in cancer cell lines. Binding is also different from changing function: a compound can inhibit an enzyme, activate a receptor or deliver a payload, and a binder can leave the target's activity unchanged. Binding assays test an interaction under specified conditions and engagement assays examine the relevant cells or tissue, while a downstream signal measures a biological consequence and is not automatically a direct measure of how much of the target is occupied; growth, death and regrowth assays add further layers. A measured change in signalling, division or survival needs controls that test the proposed explanation, and one positive experiment should not carry the whole claim.

The last step is clinical. Mechanistic plausibility does not show benefit, because the target may also be present in healthy tissue and the useful margin depends on achieved benefit and harm in a stated disease, treatment setting, product and outcome. The National Cancer Institute adds that cancer cells can become resistant to targeted therapy when the target itself changes so the drug can no longer interact with it, or when cells find new ways to grow that do not depend on the target.

Worked example, fictional. An antibody binds protein A on cancer cells, and a growth assay shows no change. Binding is supported under the assay conditions. It has not been shown that protein A drives growth, that the antibody inhibits protein A's function, that a finished payload-bearing product delivers anything, or that the product is safe and beneficial; each of those needs its own evidence. Before saying a drug worked, name the layer that was measured.

A drug target is a biological molecule or structure that a treatment acts on, and the mechanism of action explains how that action produces an effect. The National Cancer Institute describes targeted therapy as treatment that targets proteins that control how cancer cells grow, divide and spread, and says most targeted therapies are small-molecule drugs, which are small enough to enter cells and so suit targets inside cells, or monoclonal antibodies, which are designed to attach to specific targets on cancer cells. It describes antibodies that mark cancer cells for the immune system, antibodies that stop growth or cause self-destruction directly, and antibodies that carry toxins to cancer cells. These are different jobs, so a shared label of targeted does not make the mechanisms interchangeable, and a target that is only an address for delivery need not drive the cancer's growth.

An altered gene or an elevated protein can suggest a target hypothesis; it does not show that inhibiting the target will harm cancer cells selectively, which controlled perturbations of the target test, and safe exposure and appropriate clinical studies answer later questions. Naming a target answers only the first of several questions. Binding is an interaction between molecules and can be shown with a purified protein, which does not show that the compound reaches the protein inside a cell. Target engagement asks whether the interaction occurs in the relevant cells or tissue, and exposure, target location and the cell membrane all bear on it; a blood concentration and a concentration at an intracellular target are different observations. The cellular thermal shift assay of Martinez Molina and colleagues was developed to evaluate drug binding to target proteins in cells and tissue samples, and its authors used it to monitor drug transport and activation, off-target effects and resistance in cancer cell lines. Binding is also different from changing function: a compound can inhibit an enzyme, activate a receptor or deliver a payload, and a binder can leave the target's activity unchanged. Binding assays test an interaction under specified conditions and engagement assays examine the relevant cells or tissue, while a downstream signal measures a biological consequence and is not automatically a direct measure of how much of the target is occupied; growth, death and regrowth assays add further layers. A measured change in signalling, division or survival needs controls that test the proposed explanation, and one positive experiment should not carry the whole claim.

The last step is clinical. Mechanistic plausibility does not show benefit, because the target may also be present in healthy tissue and the useful margin depends on achieved benefit and harm in a stated disease, treatment setting, product and outcome. The National Cancer Institute adds that cancer cells can become resistant to targeted therapy when the target itself changes so the drug can no longer interact with it, or when cells find new ways to grow that do not depend on the target.

Worked example, fictional. An antibody binds protein A on cancer cells, and a growth assay shows no change. Binding is supported under the assay conditions. It has not been shown that protein A drives growth, that the antibody inhibits protein A's function, that a finished payload-bearing product delivers anything, or that the product is safe and beneficial; each of those needs its own evidence. Before saying a drug worked, name the layer that was measured.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
A chemical probe is a research compound used to perturb a defined biological process in cells or animals. It is useful only to the extent that it is potent enough, selective enough and characterised well enough for the question being asked. Arrowsmith and colleagues put the requirement as a probe that is potent, of known selectivity and with a proven mechanism of action, and describe how many probes in common use were first characterised inadequately and later proved to be nonselective. LY294002 was described in 1994 as a selective inhibitor of PI3 kinase and was still sold as one by nearly all vendors, although by 2005 it was clear that it inhibited many other proteins at the concentrations used to inhibit PI3 kinase. An effect seen in cells at a high concentration therefore identifies an effect at that concentration, not necessarily a target.

The numerical standards belong to the groups that set them. For probes of epigenetic targets, the Structural Genomics Consortium as described by Arrowsmith and colleagues asks minimally for in vitro potency at the target below 100 nM, more than 30-fold selectivity over related proteins of the same family, profiling against a standard panel of off-targets and effects on the target in cells below 1 uM, and now requires an inactive close analogue as a negative control. Workman and Collins advocate assessing fitness for the intended experiment rather than applying an overly restrictive universal rule. Those cut-offs were written for particular target classes and do not apply to every probe, and neither paper offers a number that makes a concentration universally clean.

Controls carry the causal argument. An inactive or weakly active analogue from the same chemical family asks whether the effect follows the target-binding feature rather than shared chemistry; an active probe of a different chemical structure asks whether an independent perturbation agrees, with the limit that two probes can still share an off-target; and a genetic change or engineered resistance asks whether altering the target alters the effect as predicted, with the limit that removing a whole protein is different from blocking one of its functions. Workman and Collins add that a chemical probe can inhibit a specific function rather than remove the protein, which RNA interference cannot, and that both approaches have off-target as well as on-target effects. Agreement among these tests strengthens an inference, and conflicts should be recorded rather than set aside.

A probe is not a medicine. Arrowsmith and colleagues note that a probe does not need to meet the requirements of a successful medicine, such as good pharmacodynamics and oral bioavailability, and that high-quality probes have served as seeds for new medicines. A medicine also needs evidence in people about product quality, exposure, tolerability and benefit for its intended use, so a useful probe may lack adequate delivery, stability or safety, and an approved medicine can be a poor tool for isolating one target if several of its interactions contribute to its effects; this is an evidence-reading distinction rather than a claim that the same experiment establishes clinical suitability. A culture concentration is not a patient dose.

Target engagement is the separate question of whether a compound interacts with its target where the experiment needs it. The cellular thermal shift assay, introduced by Martinez Molina and colleagues, is built on ligand-induced thermal stabilisation of target proteins and was used to monitor drug binding in cells and tissue samples; a shift can support engagement under the assay conditions and is not by itself an inhibition or occupancy percentage. Dose is the amount of a named medicine, in stated units. Dosage adds the interval between administrations and the duration of treatment. Cumulative dose is the total amount given, and dose intensity is that medicine's amount per defined unit of time. These quantities do not directly measure concentration at a target or clinical benefit.

FDA's August 2024 oncology dosage-optimisation guidance recommends using exposure, activity, safety and tolerability to select and compare dosages during clinical development. It describes the historical maximum-tolerated-dose approach, but a higher tolerated dose does not by itself establish a better balance of benefit and harm. These are nonbinding recommendations with stated modality and development limits. The effects of a reduction, delay or interruption depend on the medicine, regimen and reason for the change.

In the fictional four-dose example, both schedules use the same Drug Z and formulation. The first window is week 0 up to week 4, with administrations at weeks 0, 1, 2 and 3; the second is week 0 up to week 8, with administrations at weeks 0, 2, 4 and 6. Each declared window includes one nominal final interval and no administration at its right endpoint. Both totals are 40 arbitrary units, but the intensities are 10 and 5 units per week. A different final-cycle convention needs its own definition. Cumulative dose retains amount units; intensity adds a time denominator; relative intensity is the dimensionless ratio to a stated reference.

Dose, dosage, cumulative dose and dose intensity are different quantities. Dose is the quantity of drug (state the drug, the formulation and whether it is per administration or per day; milligrams, milligrams per kilogram and milligrams per square metre are different scales), and dosage is the dose with its schedule, meaning the interval between doses and the duration of treatment (FDA, 'Optimizing the Dosage of Human Prescription Drugs and Biological Products for the Treatment of Oncologic Diseases', August 2024, which says it does not specifically address several modalities). Cumulative dose adds the amounts given over a course. Dose intensity is the amount of a named drug delivered per unit time, commonly milligrams per square metre per week, and relative dose intensity divides delivered by a stated reference intensity, so it needs the reference regimen and method named; a delay lowers delivered intensity in the same proportion as an equal dose reduction, and the link between delivered intensity and response or survival has not been fully demonstrated (Alberto 1995). Equal milligrams of different medicines are not equivalent activity, and a body-size-normalised dose is not a laboratory concentration. Teaching arithmetic with invented units, not data: four 10-unit administrations over a 4-week window give 40 units and 10 units per week; the same four over 8 weeks give 5 units per week, 50 per cent of the first intensity, which says nothing about benefit, exposure or safety.

In the fictional four-dose example, both schedules use the same Drug Z and formulation. The first window is week 0 up to week 4, with administrations at weeks 0, 1, 2 and 3; the second is week 0 up to week 8, with administrations at weeks 0, 2, 4 and 6. Each declared window includes one nominal final interval and no administration at its right endpoint. Both totals are 40 arbitrary units, but the intensities are 10 and 5 units per week. A different final-cycle convention needs its own definition. Cumulative dose retains amount units; intensity adds a time denominator; relative intensity is the dimensionless ratio to a stated reference.

Pharmacokinetics describes absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion. A dose is an administered amount; exposure describes a named substance's concentration over time in a specified compartment. Route, organ function, metabolism, binding and interactions can make equal doses produce different exposure.

The December 2016 FDA labelling guidance asks for measures such as maximum plasma concentration, concentration-time area under the curve, clearance, accumulation and half-life in their relevant conditions. These measurements inform dosage selection alongside activity, safety and tolerability; they do not establish benefit on their own. For conjugated drugs, active metabolites and radiopharmaceuticals, specify which component was measured. Blood concentration is not automatically the concentration of active material at a cancer-cell target.

A drug's half-life describes a halving of the concentration of a named substance in a specified phase or model. Early distribution, terminal elimination and the effective half-life relevant to accumulation can differ. With nonlinear elimination, a reported value can also depend on the dose. The December 2016 FDA clinical-pharmacology labelling guidance distinguishes effective from terminal half-life and asks for the conditions needed to interpret each.

Concentration and effect need separate measurements. Active metabolites, persistent biological changes and tissue injury can matter after the measured parent drug has declined. Living cell products can expand rather than simply disappear, and a radiopharmaceutical combines physical decay with biological removal. A half-life alone supplies no universal treatment schedule or recovery clock.

A fictional population starts with 990 sensitive and 10 resistant cells, total 1,000. Removing 90 per cent of the sensitive cells leaves 99 sensitive plus 10 resistant cells, total 109. The resistant share rises from 10/1,000 = 1 per cent to 10/109, about 9.2 per cent, although the absolute resistant count stays at 10. No division, mutation or state switching is included. To display this honestly, compare absolute counts on one 0 to 1,000 scale and resistant fractions on a separately labelled 0 to 10 per cent scale. A larger fraction alone does not prove growth of that population, a newly induced mutation or a clinical treatment effect.

Drug resistance describes reduced treatment effect in a specified setting. Primary and acquired resistance describe the timing of response, rather than proving a single biological cause. Changes in the target, alternative signalling, drug handling and reversible cell states can contribute. Sampling, exposure and controlled functional evidence are needed to distinguish a plausible explanation from a demonstrated treatment-specific mechanism.

Drug resistance is reduced effect for a specified medicine, cancer population and setting. A garden analogy can describe selection: removing susceptible plants leaves a larger share of survivors, without showing that the treatment created those survivors. Intrinsic resistance describes poor initial effect; acquired resistance describes lost effect after an earlier response. These timing labels do not identify one permanent mechanism. A rare pre-existing population can become easier to detect, and sequence change, reversible cell state, exposure and the surrounding tissue can contribute together.

Sharma 2010 found small drug-tolerant populations in human cancer-cell cultures. In PC9 lung cancer cells, persisters propagated without drug regained sensitivity within nine doublings; expanded persister populations required roughly 90 doublings or 20 to 30 passages. The observations supported a reversible chromatin-associated state in those systems, distinct from assuming a new permanent resistance mutation. They do not establish that a treatment break is safe or beneficial for a person. Drug withdrawal and re-exposure are experimental tests of reversibility, with matched conditions and controls.

Combining drugs is a hypothesis that must address the measured failure at useful exposures and tolerable harm. NCI notes both the rationale for combinations and the possibility of serious targeted-treatment side effects. Different pathway targets do not guarantee nonoverlapping toxicity or clinical rescue. A later variant found in a fictional progression sample is especially hard to interpret if the earlier sample lacked enough coverage to detect it: it may have been present but undetected, arisen later or be unrelated to the observed failure. First check the comparison and detection limit, then test its treatment-specific function. Detection, origin, timing and causation are separate conclusions.

The two fictional comparisons use different units of inference. In a ten-tumour better-component model, A covers tumours 1 to 4 and B covers 3 to 6: 4 + 4 - 2 = 6 in the union, with four in neither group. There is no extra within-tumour interaction or added toxicity in that counting model. Separately, one cultured-cell experiment at 72 hours gives 20%, 30% and 40% inhibition for A, B and the pair at one fixed dose pair. Inhibition here is a reduction in vehicle-normalised viable-cell count, not a direct death measurement. HSA expects 30% and Bliss 44%, so 40% exceeds the first and falls below the second. Loewe needs single-drug dose-response curves; three numbers and no uncertainty estimate cannot establish a general synergy claim. In this model, greater overlap among responders reduces the union. Independent drug action does not require the two response groups to be statistically independent; shared resistance and response correlation matter to a population prediction.

Reading a combination result. A combination rationale should name the job of each component (for example a growth pathway, a survival route, a location or stage, or a resistant population), and each story makes predictions that need testing. A regimen that beats one component does not show which component supplied the benefit, nor superiority to every alternative. In ASCENT-04 (443 people with previously untreated locally advanced or metastatic triple-negative breast cancer whose tumours express PD-L1, combined positive score 10 or higher), median progression-free survival was 11.2 months with sacituzumab govitecan plus pembrolizumab and 7.8 months with physician's-choice chemotherapy plus pembrolizumab (hazard ratio 0.65, 95 per cent CI 0.51 to 0.84; label section 14); that compares the ADC with chemotherapy as pembrolizumab's partner and does not by itself show synergy. Independent drug action offers another explanation: if each person benefits from the drug to which their tumour is most sensitive, patient-to-patient variability alone can explain the superiority of many approved combinations without additivity or synergy (Palmer and Sorger), which is an alternative explanation, not a rule that effective combinations lack synergy. A combination can also add toxicity, change exposure or force lower doses, and simultaneous and sequential treatment are different strategies that a molecular diagram cannot choose between.

What 'synergy' means and how it is measured. Synergy is the narrower claim that a combined effect exceeds a stated reference expectation, and the references differ. Highest single agent (Gaddum) expects the better single effect and is the easiest bar to clear. Bliss independence expects the probability of being unaffected by each drug to be independent, so for effects written as fractions the expectation is A plus B minus A times B. Loewe additivity treats the two drugs as dilutions of one another and needs the full dose-response curve of each, with straight-line isoboles as its classic form. In Chou's median-effect method a combination index below 1 indicates synergism, equal to 1 additivity and above 1 antagonism, within that method only. Meyer et al. found no consensus on how to quantify synergy, and Yadav et al. note that a drug combined with itself can easily exceed the highest single agent and that their zero-interaction potency score is zero when both independence and dose additivity hold. A 2020 review's point stands: a synergy claim needs its model, scale and uncertainty named. Greco's 1995 review was identified but only its title could be read. Laboratory interaction analysis needs single-drug dose-response data, combination conditions, controls and variation estimates; a clinical survival advantage does not by itself measure a cell-level interaction.

Synthetic lethality is a lethal interaction between two impairments, each of which can be tolerated alone in the tested system. One impairment may already be present in a cancer and an experimental intervention can create the second, so the concept does not require two drugs. Genetic identity, loss of function, target engagement and the lethal outcome each need evidence.

The 2005 Farmer and Bryant studies found sensitivity to PARP inhibition in BRCA-impaired experimental systems. Murai and colleagues later distinguished PARP trapping from catalytic inhibition. These findings support particular mechanisms; they do not make every BRCA-related finding a clinical selection rule. Candidate pairs such as MTAP with PRMT5, mismatch-repair deficiency with WRN, or repair deficiency with POLQ need their own model, exposure, selectivity and clinical evidence.

A fictional test uses matched cultures over the same interval: neither impairment, A alone, B alone and A plus B. Each single impairment is tolerated and only the pair causes death measured by a validated assay, with independent perturbations reproducing it. In a separate rescue culture, restoring A while B remains impaired reduces death; this tests attribution and does not revive already dead cells. If a short assay instead shows fewer cells, slower division and cell loss remain unresolved. Other cell backgrounds and normal cells are separate tests of context and selectivity.

What has to be shown. Compare matched cells with neither impairment, each alone and both, and check that the intended functions changed. Measure death separately from slower growth, because a viability signal can fall when cells divide less or change metabolism; pair a suitable death assay with long-term survival or colony formation, and record concentration, time and denominator, remembering that colony formation measures reproductive survival and not the way cells die. Synthetic lethality is not oncogene addiction, which is dependence on an active driver: in Src-, BCR-ABL- and EGF receptor-dependent cells, unequal attenuation of survival and pro-apoptotic signals after the driver is inactivated contributes to death (Sharma et al.). It is also not synergy, since a score above a reference model does not identify which losses interact. In the BRCA/PARP example, homologous recombination is a DNA repair process and HRD means deficiency of that process. Trapping PARP on DNA and inhibiting its catalytic activity are different perturbations, while repair restoration or changes in replication stress can change sensitivity. The first impairment can pre-exist, so a two-loss interaction does not require two drugs.

Rescue, restoration and what each test can show. A rescue experiment restores a relevant function and asks whether the predicted harm falls; that strengthens attribution, but a failed rescue is not automatic disproof, because the restored function may not be expressed, localised or timed adequately (a reading rule, not a result from these experiments). A real example of functional restoration involved secondary BRCA2 mutations, often described as reversions. Ovarian cancer lines PEO1, PEO4 and PEO6 came from one BRCA2 mutation carrier: PEO1 was BRCA2 deficient and sensitive to cisplatin and a PARP inhibitor, while a secondary BRCA2 mutation that cancelled the inherited one arose in the patient (PEO4, PEO6) and, under cisplatin and PARP-inhibitor selection of PEO1, in the dish, restoring BRCA2 and resistance. Function was shown by homologous recombination assays after transfecting wild-type or mutant BRCA2 cDNA into reporter cells, and transient siRNA depletion (two siRNAs against a non-targeting control) re-sensitised the restored clones and PEO4 (Sakai et al. 2009). That is a secondary-mutation restoration plus knockdown in one patient's lineage, not a designed rescue of a knockout, and depleting a protein is not the same as inhibiting it with a drug. BRCA and PARP evidence is experimental: BRCA1 or BRCA2 dysfunction sensitised cells to PARP inhibition (Farmer et al.), BRCA2-deficient cells and tumours were acutely sensitive (Bryant et al.), and PARP inhibitors trap PARP1 and PARP2 on damaged DNA, with trapping potency (niraparib above olaparib, far above veliparib) not tracking catalytic inhibition (Murai et al.). Normal tissue can share the vulnerability: normal Brca2-deficient mouse intestinal epithelium showed very high apoptosis within hours of PARP inhibition (Hay et al.). None of this establishes clinical benefit.

A drug target is a biological molecule or structure that a treatment acts on, and the mechanism of action explains how that action produces an effect. The National Cancer Institute describes targeted therapy as treatment that targets proteins that control how cancer cells grow, divide and spread, and says most targeted therapies are small-molecule drugs, which are small enough to enter cells and so suit targets inside cells, or monoclonal antibodies, which are designed to attach to specific targets on cancer cells. It describes antibodies that mark cancer cells for the immune system, antibodies that stop growth or cause self-destruction directly, and antibodies that carry toxins to cancer cells. These are different jobs, so a shared label of targeted does not make the mechanisms interchangeable, and a target that is only an address for delivery need not drive the cancer's growth.

An altered gene or an elevated protein can suggest a target hypothesis; it does not show that inhibiting the target will harm cancer cells selectively, which controlled perturbations of the target test, and safe exposure and appropriate clinical studies answer later questions. Naming a target answers only the first of several questions. Binding is an interaction between molecules and can be shown with a purified protein, which does not show that the compound reaches the protein inside a cell. Target engagement asks whether the interaction occurs in the relevant cells or tissue, and exposure, target location and the cell membrane all bear on it; a blood concentration and a concentration at an intracellular target are different observations. The cellular thermal shift assay of Martinez Molina and colleagues was developed to evaluate drug binding to target proteins in cells and tissue samples, and its authors used it to monitor drug transport and activation, off-target effects and resistance in cancer cell lines. Binding is also different from changing function: a compound can inhibit an enzyme, activate a receptor or deliver a payload, and a binder can leave the target's activity unchanged. Binding assays test an interaction under specified conditions and engagement assays examine the relevant cells or tissue, while a downstream signal measures a biological consequence and is not automatically a direct measure of how much of the target is occupied; growth, death and regrowth assays add further layers. A measured change in signalling, division or survival needs controls that test the proposed explanation, and one positive experiment should not carry the whole claim.

The last step is clinical. Mechanistic plausibility does not show benefit, because the target may also be present in healthy tissue and the useful margin depends on achieved benefit and harm in a stated disease, treatment setting, product and outcome. The National Cancer Institute adds that cancer cells can become resistant to targeted therapy when the target itself changes so the drug can no longer interact with it, or when cells find new ways to grow that do not depend on the target.

Worked example, fictional. An antibody binds protein A on cancer cells, and a growth assay shows no change. Binding is supported under the assay conditions. It has not been shown that protein A drives growth, that the antibody inhibits protein A's function, that a finished payload-bearing product delivers anything, or that the product is safe and beneficial; each of those needs its own evidence. Before saying a drug worked, name the layer that was measured.
